pages.observedMeaningfulContent: Lecture 18 title, Mechanism Design I, with author/institution identification and a campus image.
Learning outcomes list task-driven design, DOF, workspace/load/speed/accuracy requirements, configurations, wrists, quantitative indices and Python workspace plotting.
Contents page organizes task requirements, configurations, quantitative workspace attributes and the programming example.
Physical design affects kinematic/dynamic complexity and closed-form solvability. Four system parts are listed. The drawing distinguishes the articulated manipulator from the distal end-effector.

Programmability does not imply universal task optimality. Heavy automotive welding and fast circuit assembly motivate different compromises. Joint count, arrangement, actuation and sensing are iterative decisions.

DOF is the number of independent configuration variables. Typical serial one-DOF joints are contrasted with closed-loop mobility criteria. The three-rotation drawing labels the base, middle and distal motions. The sentence calling every task mismatch redundant is overbroad.

General spatial pose has three position and three orientation coordinates. Task-relative redundancy is illustrated by an axially symmetric tool whose roll can be irrelevant; reachability and actual task symmetry remain necessary qualifications.

Workspace means reachable end-effector volume. Size, shape, singularities and structural/fixture interference matter. The three-dimensional point-cloud drawing is illustrative; its tiny cursor coordinates are not stated problem data.

Load depends on link strength/stiffness, transmission and actuator output, configuration and dynamics. Whole-workspace guaranteed capacity must be distinguished from the allowable load at a particular configuration.
Peak speed is not cycle time. Short pick-and-place moves can be acceleration/deceleration limited. Painting or welding can impose a process-limited useful travel rate.

Repeatability means returning consistently to a taught point; accuracy means reaching a mathematical target. Manufacturing tolerances and kinematic calibration matter. The 0.001-inch versus 8±2-inch spray example motivates task-appropriate precision and cost.

The common arm–wrist partition separates first-three-joint wrist positioning from the remaining orientation motions. Intersecting axes, zero dimensions and 0/±90-degree twists can simplify kinematics. The drawing highlights the arm and wrist portions.

Cartesian positioning uses three perpendicular prismatic axes, giving a rectangular/box workspace. The side view labels vertical travel d₂ and horizontal travel d₃; the top view shows d₁. The ideal independent positioning map has full rank. Stiff gantry construction suits heavy tasks.

Cartesian designs combine rigidity and payload capability with linear-actuator speed limits and simple position inverse kinematics. Fixtures/feeders must fit the surrounding structure; this can complicate retrofit. The singularity claim concerns the positioning substructure.

Articulated, jointed, elbow and anthropomorphic describe the arm arrangement. Shoulder yaw and elevation plus a parallel-axis elbow produce a complex nearly spherical envelope. The diagrams show curved restricted sectors. Boundary and internal alignments can be singular.

Typical cantilevered articulated structures are less stiff but less intrusive than Cartesian structures, aiding confined access. Cost and inverse-kinematics/control comparisons are design-dependent, not universal orderings.

SCARA is expanded as Selectively Compliant Assembly Robot Arm. Three parallel revolute motions and normal prismatic motion support planar assembly with height and yaw. Prose calls the prismatic joint fourth, while the figure labels d₃. The Adept One date, speed and priority statements are source-attributed historical examples, not verified universal benchmarks.

Base-mounted first-two actuators reduce moving mass. Vertical stiffness and horizontal compliance support assembly/insertion. Equal planar links are often chosen. The wording about joints not supporting weight must distinguish zero vertical-axis gravity torque from nonzero structural support loads.

Spherical positioning replaces the articulated elbow rotation with radial extension. The figure labels azimuth θ₁, elevation θ₂ and radial d₃, giving a shell/wedge region. Retraction can require rear clearance. Symmetric-tool suitability does not imply arbitrary spatial pose control.

Cylindrical positioning independently controls height, azimuth and radial reach. The figure labels θ₁, d₂ and d₃, while the prose enumerates the motions in a different order. Side and top sections are rectangular and annular-sector shaped. Vertical/radial material handling is the stated application.

The orienting wrist follows the positioning arm. The diagram places θ₄–θ₆ in the wrist. Conventional orthogonal-axis orientation reach assumes no joint limits, not absence of singularities. Non-orthogonal three-roll wrists can offer continuous joint rotation.

The non-orthogonal-wrist continuation describes an unattainable orientation cone. A separate picture is explicitly captioned as an orthogonal wrist remotely driven through three concentric shafts A₄–A₆. The broad intersecting-axis closed-form claim is retained only with explicit scope.

The structural length sum is Σ(a_(i−1)+d_i). The prismatic contribution is full travel, not the current coordinate. Numerical interpretations use nonnegative physical lengths; signed DH cancellation is not silently assumed.

The structural length index is L/W^(1/3), using positive three-dimensional workspace volume. Smaller ratios favor length efficiency only. Equal Cartesian travels give the ideal minimum 3.0; 0.62 is an ideal articulated benchmark, not a universal guarantee.

Task singularity is Jacobian rank loss. det(J)=0 applies to square J. Manipulability is √det(JJᵀ), reducing to |det J| for square J. Conditioning and directional uniformity are not fully described by the determinant product alone.

The inertia discussion attributed to Asada uses M_x=J^(−T)MJ^(−1), requiring square nonsingular J. The normalized quadratic form XᵀM_xX=1 gives an inertia metric ellipsoid. Equal principal values give isotropy. The figure displays changing local ellipse shapes and directions, not prescribed trajectories or universal actuator-limited acceleration bounds.

The programming problem specifies an ideal planar 2R arm with lengths 5 and 4 and both angles from −π to π. The fixed-frame FK uses θ₁ for the first link and θ₁+θ₂ for the second. No named physical length unit is supplied.

The diagram labels base-to-elbow length l₁, elbow-to-tool length l₂, base angle θ₁ and relative elbow angle θ₂. The equations substitute lengths 5 and 4 without changing the relative-angle convention.

The continuous ideal workspace is the annulus 1≤r≤9. The inner and outer bounds are the difference and sum of link lengths. The text describes plotted points as all positions; finite sampling must be distinguished from the continuous reachable set.

The actual code uses two inclusive 200-point linspaces, nested loops, and paired coordinate lists. It generates 40,000 evaluations. The even grid omits zero and includes periodically equivalent endpoints. The ordinary title string visually wraps across lines, requiring explicit repair for literal execution. Figure size, marker size, equal aspect, labels, grid and show have distinct roles.

The output has an inner hole of radius about 1, outer reach about 9, equal axis scale, and finite sampling rings/gaps. Red arrows indicate inner and outer radii. Blank regions between finite markers do not establish extra continuous-workspace obstacles.

The summary combines task-dependent requirements, configuration choice, structural and manipulability metrics, and FK workspace visualization. These are linked to the earlier concepts rather than padded with a duplicate summary quiz.
